Income Taxes  
The Company accounts for income taxes under the asset and liability method, which requires the recognition of deferred tax assets and liabilities for the expected future tax consequences of events that have been included in the consolidated financial statements. Under this method, deferred tax assets and liabilities are determined on the basis of the differences between the consolidated financial statements and tax basis of assets and liabilities using enacted tax rates in effect for the year or years in which the differences are expected to reverse. The effect of a change in the tax rates on deferred tax assets and liabilities is recognized in income in the period that includes the enactment date of such change.  
The Company recognizes deferred tax assets to the extent that it believes these assets are more likely than not to be realized. In making such a determination, the Company considers all available positive and negative evidence, including future reversals of existing taxable temporary differences, projected future taxable income, tax planning strategies, and the Company’s recent operating results. The Company establishes a valuation allowance when it does not consider it more likely than not that a deferred tax asset will be recovered.  
The Company records uncertain tax positions on the basis of a two-step process whereby (1) the Company determines whether it is more likely than not that the tax positions will be sustained on the basis of the technical merits of the position and (2) for those tax positions that meet the more-likely-than-not recognition threshold, the Company recognizes the largest amount of tax benefit that is more than 50% likely to be realized upon ultimate settlement with the related tax authority.  
Interest and/or penalties related to uncertain tax positions are recognized in the income tax provision.  
Measurement of Defined Benefit Pension and Other Postretirement Employee Benefit Plans  
The Company sponsors defined benefit pension plans (“pension plans”) and other postretirement employee benefit plans (“OPEB plans”) for its employees and retirees. The Company recognizes the funded status of its pension and OPEB plans on the consolidated balance sheets based on the year-end measurements of plan assets and benefit obligations. When the fair value of plan assets are in excess of the plan benefit obligations, the amounts are reported in other current assets and other assets. When the fair value of plan benefit obligations are in excess of plan assets, the amounts are reported in accrued expenses and other long-term liabilities based on the amount by which the actuarial present value of benefits payable in the next twelve months included in the benefit obligation exceeds the fair value of plan assets. The net periodic benefit income for the Company’s pension and OPEB plans do not contain a service cost component as these plans have been frozen for an extended period of time. Non-service cost components of pension and postretirement net periodic benefit income are included in other income in the consolidated statements of operations.

The preparation of the consolidated financial statements requires certain assets and liabilities to be measured at fair value. Financial instruments measured at fair value are classified based on inputs within a three-level hierarchy established by GAAP: Level 1 includes unadjusted quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets; Level 2 includes valuation inputs other than Level 1 based on observable market data, such as quoted prices for similar assets in active markets, quoted prices for identical assets in inactive markets, observable interest rates and credit risks, or valuation inputs derived from or corroborated by observable markets; Level 3 includes inputs developed from unobservable data reflecting the Company’s assumptions. Financial assets and liabilities are classified based on the lowest level of input that is significant to the valuation. When quoted prices in active markets for identical assets and liabilities are available, the Company uses these prices and classifies the instruments in Level 1. In other cases where quoted prices are not available or not observable, the Company estimates fair value using valuation methodologies based on available and observable market information or a matrix pricing model, classifying these instruments in Level 2. If quoted market prices are not available, the Company determines fair value using broker quotes or internal models.

Financial assets and liabilities are classified based on the lowest level of input that is significant to their valuation. Level 1 includes unadjusted quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets. Level 2 includes valuation inputs other than Level 1 that are based on observable market data, such as quoted prices for similar assets in active markets, quoted prices for identical assets in inactive markets, observable interest rates and credit risks, or valuation inputs derived from or corroborated by observable markets. Level 3 includes inputs that are unobservable and developed from the Company’s own assumptions. When quoted prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets are available, the Company uses those prices and classifies the assets or liabilities in Level 1. If such prices are not available or not observable, the Company estimates fair value using valuation methodologies based on observable market information or a matrix pricing model, classifying these in Level 2. For financial assets and liabilities without observable inputs, the Company uses broker quotes or internal analysis of financial performance and cash flow projections, which may result in Level 3 classification even if some significant inputs are observable. Cash and cash equivalents have carrying values that approximate fair value due to maturities of less than three months; when quoted prices are available in active markets, they are classified in Level 1; otherwise, they are classified in Level 2. Debt securities with quoted prices in active markets are classified in Level 1, primarily consisting of U.S. Treasury securities. Level 2 debt securities use models like matrix pricing or discounted cash flows, with prices based on observable market inputs such as quoted prices for similar assets, interest rates, and credit risks. The Company reviews these prices quarterly, compares them to secondary sources, and validates any variances over a specified threshold. The Company’s internal investment team also independently compares prices to its own estimates. No prices were adjusted for Level 2 debt securities at December 31, 2022 or 2021. CMS regularly audits the Company’s compliance with regulations and contracts, using payment mechanisms that consider member health status based on provider-submitted data, and pays increased premiums to Medicare Advantage and PDP plans for members with certain conditions. CMS conducts risk adjustment data validation (RADV) audits to validate coding and medical record documentation, and may require the Company to refund premiums if risk-adjusted payments are not properly supported. In 2012, CMS revised its RADV audit methodology for contract years 2011 and forward, introducing extrapolation of sample error rates and a FFS Adjuster, which increased the Company’s exposure to refunds due to incomplete medical records. From 2011 to 2013, CMS conducted only a few contract-level RADV audits. In October 2018, CMS proposed a new RADV methodology targeting health conditions and members with multiple diagnoses, using extrapolation without a FFS Adjuster, and initiated audits for 2014 and 2015 under this methodology before a final rule. On January 30, 2023, CMS released the final RADV Audit Rule, allowing extrapolation for payment years 2018 and forward for both RADV and OIG audits and eliminating the FFS Adjuster in Part C contract-level RADV audits. The rule indicates CMS will use multiple audit methodologies and audit contracts at highest risk based on statistical modeling, citing a 2016 GAO report recommending focus on high overpayment risk, high coding intensity, and high unsupported diagnoses. The Company’s disclosure controls and procedures are designed to ensure that material information relating to the Company and its consolidated subsidiaries is made known to the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer on a timely basis. Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting, which includes policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the Company’s assets; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of the Company’s consolidated financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the Company are made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of the Company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company’s assets that could have a material effect on the Company’s consolidated financial statements. Management assessed the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022, based on the criteria established in the Internal Control-Integrated Framework issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (2013 framework), and concluded that the Company’s internal control over financial reporting is effective and provides reasonable assurance that assets are safeguarded and that the financial records are reliable for preparing financial statements as of that date. There are inherent limitations in the effectiveness of any system of internal control over financial reporting. There has been no change in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting during the fourth quarter ended December 31, 2022 that has materially affected, or is reasonably likely to materially affect, the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. As of February 8, 2023, the authorized capital stock of CVS Health Corporation consists of (i) 3,200,000,000 shares of common stock, par value of $0.01 per share, (ii) 120,619 shares of cumulative preferred stock, par value $0.01 per share, and (iii) 50,000,000 shares of preference stock, par value $1.00 per share. Holders of common stock are entitled to one vote per share on all matters voted on by stockholders, including director elections, and exclusively possess all voting power except as otherwise required by law, preferred stock provisions, or board resolutions. The Charter precludes cumulative voting in director elections and provides for a majority vote standard for uncontested director elections and a plurality vote standard for contested elections. Subject to any rights of outstanding preferred or preference stock, holders of common stock are entitled to dividends declared from funds available therefor, no dividends may be declared on common stock unless full cumulative dividends are paid on any outstanding preferred stock and any other preferred stock designated to have such dividend preference, and upon dissolution, holders of common stock are entitled to receive pro rata all assets available for distribution, subject to any liquidation preferences of preferred or preference stock. The Charter provides that no holder of any class or series of shares has preemptive rights to purchase or subscribe for any shares or securities convertible into shares of CVS Health. Under Delaware law, stockholders have the right to adopt, amend, or repeal the Charter and By-Laws, but any amendment to the Charter must be approved by the board. Amendments to the Charter require a majority vote of all stockholders entitled to vote thereon, or a majority of votes cast in each class vote if any class or series is entitled to vote. The By-Laws may be amended by the board for all matters not exclusively reserved by law to stockholders, and amendments to the By-Laws may be adopted by the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote at an annual or special meeting or by a majority of directors present at a regular or special meeting with a quorum. Certain provisions of the Charter and By-Laws may have an antitakeover effect and may delay, defer, or prevent a tender offer or takeover attempt, including the authority to issue preferred or preference stock with designations, preferences, rights, qualifications, limitations, or restrictions as the board may determine, such as dividend status, redemption rights, liquidation preferences, conversion rights, and restrictions on issuance.

The authorized capital stock of CVS Health, including preferred stock, preference stock, and common stock, is available for issuance without further action by CVS Health stockholders, unless required by applicable law or the rules of any stock exchange or automated quotation system on which CVS Health’s securities are listed or traded. If stockholder approval is not required, the board does not intend to seek such approval. Although the board has no current intention to do so, it could issue a class or series of preferred stock or preference stock that, depending on its terms, might hinder a merger, tender offer, or other takeover attempt that some or a majority of CVS Health stockholders might view as beneficial or in which stockholders might receive a premium over the current market price. CVS Health does not currently have a stockholder rights plan, but the board retains the right to adopt one in the future. The Charter grants the board exclusive authority to create and issue rights that allow holders to purchase shares of capital stock or other securities from CVS Health and to elect to repurchase, redeem, terminate, or amend such rights. The timing and terms of issuance, repurchase, redemption, termination, or amendment are determined solely by the board and are set forth in the relevant contracts or instruments. The board’s authority includes setting the purchase price upon exercise, specifying when and under what circumstances rights may be exercised or transferred, including adjustments to the number or exercise price of rights or the amount or nature of securities received in the event of a combination, split, recapitalization, change in ownership, reorganization, merger, consolidation, sale of assets, or other related events, and provisions that restrict CVS Health from entering into such transactions without the other party assuming the rights’ obligations. The board may also deny the right to exercise rights to holders of a specified percentage of outstanding securities or cause such rights to become void, permit redemption or exchange of rights, and appoint a rights agent. Stockholder action may be taken by written consent instead of a meeting, provided it complies with the Charter and By-Laws, and any person other than CVS Health seeking such action must deliver a written notice signed by holders of record representing at least 25% of the voting power of outstanding capital stock entitled to express consent, requesting a record date. Under Delaware law, transactions such as a sale, lease, or exchange of all or substantially all of CVS Health’s assets, an amendment to the Charter, a merger or consolidation with another corporation, or a dissolution generally require the affirmative vote of the board and a majority of the aggregate voting power of outstanding stock entitled to vote, with limited exceptions. For transactions with related persons (those owning at least 10% of CVS Health’s outstanding capital stock), a majority of outstanding shares (excluding those owned by the related person) voting as a single class is required to approve a business combination, unless (i) the transaction is approved by a majority of continuing directors (those not affiliated with the related person or their affiliates or associates, who were on the board before the related person became a related person or whose initial election was recommended by a majority of continuing directors at the time) and who have remained in office, or (ii) certain fair price requirements are met. CVS Health has not opted out of Section 203 of the Delaware General Corporation Law, which prohibits a person who acquires 15% or more of CVS Health’s outstanding voting stock (an “interested stockholder”) from engaging in certain “business combinations” with the corporation—such as mergers, purchases or sales of 10% or more of its assets, stock purchases, or transactions increasing their ownership percentage or providing them with a financial benefit—for three years after becoming an interested stockholder, unless one of the following exceptions applies: (i) the board approved the acquisition that led to the person becoming an interested stockholder or the transaction prior to that time; (ii) upon consummation of the transaction, the person owned at least 85% of the outstanding voting stock, excluding voting stock held by directors who are also officers and certain employee stock plans; or (iii) the transaction is approved by the board and by the affirmative vote of two-thirds of the outstanding voting stock not owned by the interested stockholder. An “interested stockholder” also includes affiliates and associates of a 15% or more owner and any affiliate or associate of CVS Health who previously owned 15% or more of the outstanding voting stock within the three-year period preceding the determination.
